title: The Mystery of the Heavy Little Cube

pages.text: The Mystery of the Heavy Little Cube

Next, Ms. Romero asked the class to look closely at the size of the cubes. ‘Volume is the amount of space something takes up,’ she said. ‘These two cubes take up the same amount of space, so they have the same volume.’ Zara grinned. ‘Same volume, different mass,’ she said. ‘We are getting closer to the answer.’

Ms. Romero placed the cubes on a balance. The silver cube pulled the scale down. ‘Mass tells us how much matter an object has,’ she explained. ‘Even if two objects look alike, one can have more matter packed inside.’ Zara touched the metal cube. ‘So this one has more mass,’ she said. Eli nodded. ‘That is why it felt heavier!’

Mass is how much matter an object has. Volume is how much space an object takes up. Density is mass per unit volume, or Density = Mass ÷ Volume. Zara and Eli learned that two objects can be the same size but still have different masses. The object with more mass packed into the same volume has greater density.

Then the class tested other objects in water. A wooden block floated, but a rock sank to the bottom. ‘Density helps explain this too,’ Ms. Romero said. ‘Objects that are denser than water usually sink. Objects that are less dense than water can float.’ Zara watched the block bob at the top. ‘Density is everywhere!’

Ms. Romero wrote a new clue on the board: Density = Mass ÷ Volume. ‘Density tells how much mass is packed into each unit of space,’ she said. ‘Because the silver cube has more mass in the same volume, it is denser than the wooden cube.’ Eli smiled. ‘So density is the real mystery answer!’
